In [[geometry]], a '''snub''' is an operation applied to a [[polyhedron]]. The term originates from [[Kepler]]'s names of two [[Archimedean solid]]s, for the [[snub cube]] ({{lang|la|cubus simus}}) and [[snub dodecahedron]] ({{lang|la|dodecaedron simum}}).<ref>[[Kepler]], ''Harmonices Mundi'', 1619</ref> 

In general, snubs have [[Chirality|chiral symmetry]] with two forms: with clockwise or counterclockwise orientation. By Kepler's names, a snub can be seen as an [[Expansion (geometry)|expansion]] of a [[regular polyhedron]]: moving the faces apart, twisting them about their centers, adding new polygons centered on the original vertices, and adding pairs of triangles fitting between the original edges.

The terminology was generalized by [[Coxeter]], with a slightly different definition, for a wider set of [[uniform polytope]]s.

== Conway snubs ==
[[John Horton Conway|John Conway]] explored generalized polyhedron operators, defining what is now called [[Conway polyhedron notation]], which can be applied to polyhedra and tilings. Conway calls Coxeter's operation a ''semi-snub''.<ref>Conway, (2008) p.287 Coxeter's semi-snub operation</ref>

In this notation, [[Conway snub operator|snub]] is defined by the dual and [[Conway gyro operator|gyro]] operators, as ''s''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''dg'', and it is equivalent to an [[alternation (geometry)|alternation]] of a truncation of an [[Conway ambo operator|ambo]] operator. Conway's notation itself avoids Coxeter's alternation (half) operation since it only applies for polyhedra with even-sided faces.

In 4-dimensions, Conway suggests the [[snub 24-cell]] should be called a ''semi-snub 24-cell'' because, unlike 3-dimensional snub polyhedra are alternated omnitruncated forms, it is not an alternated [[omnitruncated 24-cell]]. It is instead actually an alternated [[truncated 24-cell]].<ref>Conway, 2008, p.401 Gosset's Semi-snub Polyoctahedron</ref>

[[Coxeter]]'s snub terminology is slightly different, meaning an [[alternation (geometry)|alternated]] [[Truncation (geometry)|truncation]], deriving the [[snub cube]] as a ''snub [[cuboctahedron]]'', and the [[snub dodecahedron]] as a ''snub [[icosidodecahedron]]''. This definition is used in the naming of two [[Johnson solid]]s: the [[snub disphenoid]] and the [[snub square antiprism]], and of higher dimensional polytopes, such as the 4-dimensional [[snub 24-cell]], with extended Schläfli symbol s{3,4,3}, and Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node_h|3|node_h|4|node|3|node}}.

A [[regular polyhedron]] (or tiling), with Schläfli symbol <math>\begin{Bmatrix} p , q \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and [[Coxeter diagram]] {{CDD|node_1|p|node|q|node}}, has [[Truncation (geometry)|truncation]] defined as <math>t \begin{Bmatrix} p , q \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and {{CDD|node_1|p|node_1|q|node}}, and has snub defined as an [[alternation (geometry)|alternated]] truncation <math>ht \begin{Bmatrix} p , q \end{Bmatrix} = s \begin{Bmatrix} p , q \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and {{CDD|node_h|p|node_h|q|node}}. This alternated construction requires ''q'' to be even.

A [[quasiregular polyhedron]], with Schläfli symbol <math>\begin{Bmatrix} p \\ q \end{Bmatrix}</math> or ''r''{''p'',''q''}, and Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node_1|split1-pq|nodes}} or {{CDD|node|p|node_1|q|node}}, has quasiregular [[Truncation (geometry)|truncation]] defined as <math>t\begin{Bmatrix} p \\ q \end{Bmatrix}</math> or ''tr''{''p'',''q''}, and {{CDD|node_1|split1-pq|nodes_11}} or {{CDD|node_1|p|node_1|q|node_1}}, and has quasiregular snub defined as an [[alternation (geometry)|alternated]] truncated rectification <math>ht\begin{Bmatrix} p \\ q \end{Bmatrix} = s\begin{Bmatrix} p \\ q \end{Bmatrix}</math> or ''htr''{''p'',''q''} = ''sr''{''p'',''q''}, and {{CDD|node_h|split1-pq|nodes_hh}} or {{CDD|node_h|p|node_h|q|node_h}}.

For example, Kepler's '''[[snub cube]]''' is derived from the quasiregular [[cuboctahedron]], with a vertical [[Schläfli symbol]] <math>\begin{Bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and [[Coxeter diagram]] {{CDD|node_1|split1-43|nodes}}, and so is more explicitly called a '''snub cuboctahedron''', expressed by a vertical Schläfli symbol <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node_h|split1-43|nodes_hh}}. The snub cuboctahedron is the alternation of the ''truncated cuboctahedron'', <math>t\begin{Bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and {{CDD|node_1|split1-43|nodes_11}}.

Regular polyhedra with even-order vertices can also be snubbed as alternated truncations, like the ''snub octahedron'', as <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} 3 , 4 \end{Bmatrix}</math>, {{CDD|node_h|3|node_h|4|node}}, is the alternation of the [[truncated octahedron]], <math>t\begin{Bmatrix} 3 , 4 \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and {{CDD|node_1|3|node_1|4|node}}. The ''snub octahedron'' represents the [[pseudoicosahedron]], a regular [[icosahedron]] with [[pyritohedral symmetry]].

The ''snub tetratetrahedron'', as <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and {{CDD|node_h|split1|nodes_hh}}, is the alternation of the truncated tetrahedral symmetry form, <math>t\begin{Bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and {{CDD|node_1|split1|nodes_11}}.

Coxeter's snub operation also allows n-[[antiprism]]s to be defined as <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} 2 \\ n \end{Bmatrix}</math> or <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} 2 , 2n \end{Bmatrix}</math>, based on n-prisms <math>t\begin{Bmatrix} 2 \\ n \end{Bmatrix}</math> or <math>t\begin{Bmatrix} 2 , 2n \end{Bmatrix}</math>, while <math>\begin{Bmatrix} 2 , n \end{Bmatrix}</math> is a regular n-[[hosohedron]], a degenerate polyhedron, but a valid tiling on the sphere with [[digon]] or [[lune (geometry)|lune]]-shaped faces.

=== Coxeter's uniform snub star-polyhedra ===
Snub star-polyhedra are constructed by their [[Schwarz triangle#Schwarz triangles for the sphere by density|Schwarz triangle]] (p q r), with rational ordered mirror-angles, and all mirrors active and alternated.

{| class=wikitable
|+ Snubbed uniform star-polyhedra

The [[great dirhombicosidodecahedron]] is also a snub, but it relates to a spherical quadrilateral (3/2 5/3 3 5/2) instead.

[[File:Great dirhombicosidodecahedron.png|100px]]

=== Coxeter's higher-dimensional snubbed polytopes and honeycombs ===
In general, a regular polychoron with [[Schläfli symbol]] <math>\begin{Bmatrix} p , q, r \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and [[Coxeter diagram]] {{CDD|node_1|p|node|q|node|r|node}}, has a snub with [[extended Schläfli symbol]] <math>s \begin{Bmatrix} p , q, r \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and {{CDD|node_h|p|node_h|q|node|r|node}}.

A rectified polychoron <math>\begin{Bmatrix} p \\ q, r \end{Bmatrix}</math> = '''r{p,q,r}''', and {{CDD|node|p|node_1|q|node|r|node}}  has snub symbol <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} p \\ q , r \end{Bmatrix}</math> = '''sr{p,q,r}''', and {{CDD|node_h|p|node_h|q|node_h|r|node}}.

=== Examples===
[[File:Ortho solid 969-uniform polychoron 343-snub.png|thumb|Orthogonal projection of [[snub 24-cell]]]]
There is only one uniform convex snub in 4-dimensions, the [[snub 24-cell]]. The regular [[24-cell]] has [[Schläfli symbol]], <math>\begin{Bmatrix} 3 , 4, 3 \end{Bmatrix}</math>, and  [[Coxeter diagram]] {{CDD|node_1|3|node|4|node|3|node}}, and the snub 24-cell is represented by <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} 3 , 4, 3 \end{Bmatrix}</math>, [[Coxeter diagram]] {{CDD|node_h|3|node_h|4|node|3|node}}. It also has an index 6 lower symmetry constructions as <math>s\left\{\begin{array}{l}3\\3\\3\end{array}\right\}</math> or s{3<sup>1,1,1</sup>} and {{CDD|node_h|splitsplit1|branch3_hh|node_h}}, and an index 3 subsymmetry as <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 , 4 \end{Bmatrix}</math> or sr{3,3,4}, and {{CDD|node_h|3|node_h|3|node_h|4|node}} or {{CDD|node_h|split1|nodes_hh|4a|nodea}}.

The related [[snub 24-cell honeycomb]] can be seen as a <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} 3 , 4, 3, 3 \end{Bmatrix}</math> or s{3,4,3,3}, and {{CDD|node_h|3|node_h|4|node|3|node|3|node}}, and lower symmetry <math>s\begin{Bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 , 4, 3 \end{Bmatrix}</math> or sr{3,3,4,3} and {{CDD|node_h|3|node_h|3|node_h|4|node|3|node}} or {{CDD|node_h|split1|nodes_hh|3a|nodea|4a|nodea}}, and lowest symmetry form as <math>s\left\{\begin{array}{l}3\\3\\3\\3\end{array}\right\}</math> or s{3<sup>1,1,1,1</sup>} and {{CDD|nodes_hh|split2|node_h|split1|nodes_hh}}.

A Euclidean honeycomb is an [[alternated hexagonal slab honeycomb]], s{2,6,3}, and {{CDD|node_h|2x|node_h|6|node|3|node}} or sr{2,3,6}, and {{CDD|node_h|2x|node_h|3|node_h|6|node}} or sr{2,3<sup>[3]</sup>}, and {{CDD|node_h|2x|node_h|split1|branch_hh}}.
: [[File:Tetroctahedric semicheck.svg|160px]]

Another Euclidean (scaliform) honeycomb is an [[alternated square slab honeycomb]], s{2,4,4}, and {{CDD|node_h|2x|node_h|4|node|4|node}} or sr{2,4<sup>1,1</sup>} and {{CDD|node_h|2x|node_h|split1-44|nodes_hh}}:
: [[File:Alternated cubic slab honeycomb.png|160px]]

The only uniform snub hyperbolic uniform honeycomb is the ''snub hexagonal tiling honeycomb'', as s{3,6,3} and {{CDD|node_h|3|node_h|6|node|3|node}}, which can also be constructed as an [[alternated hexagonal tiling honeycomb]], h{6,3,3}, {{CDD|node_h1|6|node|3|node|3|node}}. It is also constructed as s{3<sup>[3,3]</sup>} and {{CDD|branch_hh|splitcross|branch_hh}}.

Another hyperbolic (scaliform) honeycomb is a [[snub order-4 octahedral honeycomb]], s{3,4,4}, and {{CDD|node_h|3|node_h|4|node|4|node}}.
